{{Machine learning|Paradigms}}
'''Self-supervised learning''' ('''SSL''') is a paradigm in [[machine learning]] where a model is trained on a task using the data itself to generate supervisory signals, rather than relying on externally-provided labels. In the context of [[Neural network (machine learning)|neural networks]], self-supervised learning aims to leverage inherent structures or relationships within the input data to create meaningful training signals. SSL tasks are designed so that solving them requires capturing essential [[Feature (machine learning)|features]] or relationships in the data. The input data is typically augmented or transformed in a way that creates pairs of related samples, where one sample serves as the input, and the other is used to formulate the supervisory signal. This augmentation can involve introducing noise, cropping, rotation, or other transformations. Self-supervised learning more closely imitates the way humans learn to classify objects.<ref name="auto3">{{Cite web|last=Bouchard|first=Louis|date=25 November 2020|title=What is Self-Supervised Learning? {{!}} Will machines ever be able to learn like humans?|url=https://medium.com/what-is-artificial-intelligence/what-is-self-supervised-learning-will-machines-be-able-to-learn-like-humans-d9160f40cdd1|access-date=9 June 2021|website=Medium}}</ref>

During SSL, the model learns in two steps. First, the task is solved based on an auxiliary or pretext classification task using pseudo-labels, which help to initialize the model [[Parameter#Artificial intelligence|parameters]].<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Doersch|first1=Carl|last2=Zisserman|first2=Andrew|title=2017 IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV) |chapter=Multi-task Self-Supervised Visual Learning |date=October Self-supervised learning has produced promising results in recent years, and has found practical application in fields such as [[Audio signal processing|audio processing]], and is being used by [[Facebook]] and others for [[speech recognition]].<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|title=Wav2vec: State-of-the-art speech recognition through self-supervision|url=https://ai.facebook.com/blog/wav2vec-state-of-the-art-speech-recognition-through-self-supervision/|access-date=9 June 2021|website=ai.facebook.com}}</ref>

== Pseudo-labels ==
Pseudo-labels are automatically generated labels that a model assigns to unlabeled data based on its own predictions. They are widely used in self-supervised and semi-supervised learning, where ground-truth annotations are limited or unavailable. By treating predicted labels as surrogate ground truth, learning algorithms can make use of large quantities of unlabeled data in the training process.<ref name="Lee20132">{{cite conference |last=Lee |first=Dong-Hyun |year=2013 |title=Pseudo-Label: The Simple and Efficient Semi-Supervised Learning Method for Deep Neural Networks |conference=ICML 2013 Workshop on Challenges in Representation Learning (WREPL)}}</ref>

Pseudo-labeling also plays an important role in systems that must adapt to [[concept drift]], where the statistical properties of the data change over time. In these scenarios, the model may detect that an incoming instance deviates from previously learned behavior. The system then generates a classification result for that instance, and this predicted class is used as a pseudo-label for updating or retraining model components that are becoming outdated. This approach enables continuous adaptation in dynamic environments without requiring manual annotation.<ref name="Gama20142">{{cite journal |last=Gama |first=João |year=2014 |title=A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation |journal=ACM Computing Surveys |volume=46 |issue=4 |pages=1–37 |doi=10.1145/2523813 |url=http://repositorio.inesctec.pt/handle/123456789/5370 }}</ref><ref name="DroidEvolver2019">{{cite conference |last1=Xu |first1=K. |last2=Li |first2=Y. |last3=Deng |first3=R. |last4=Chen |first4=K. |last5=Xu |first5=J. |year=2019 |title=Self-Evolving Android Malware Detection System |conference=IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P) |pages=47–62 |doi=10.1109/EuroSP.2019.00014 }}</ref>

In many [[adaptive learning]] pipelines, pseudo-labels are chosen when the classifier produces sufficiently confident predictions, reducing the risk of propagating errors. These pseudo-labeled instances are then incorporated into training to refresh or evolve the model's understanding of emerging data patterns, particularly when existing components show signs of “aging” due to drift or distributional shifts. This strategy reduces reliance on manual labeling while helping maintain long-term model performance.

== Types ==

=== Autoassociative self-supervised learning ===
Autoassociative self-supervised learning is a specific category of self-supervised learning where a neural network is trained to reproduce or reconstruct its own input data.<ref name=":17">{{cite journal|doi=10.1002/aic.690370209|title=Nonlinear principal component analysis using autoassociative neural networks|journal=AIChE Journal|volume=37|issue=2|pages=233–243|date=1991|last1=Kramer|first1=Mark A.|bibcode=1991AIChE..37..233K |url= https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Abir_Alobaid/post/To_learn_a_probability_density_function_by_using_neural_network_can_we_first_estimate_density_using_nonparametric_methods_then_train_the_network/attachment/59d6450279197b80779a031e/AS:451263696510979@1484601057779/download/NL+PCA+by+using+ANN.pdf}}</ref> In other words, the model is tasked with learning a representation of the data that captures its essential features or structure, allowing it to regenerate the original input.

The term "autoassociative" comes from the fact that the model is essentially associating the input data with itself. This is often achieved using [[autoencoders]], which are a type of neural network architecture used for representation learning. Autoencoders consist of an ''encoder'' network that maps the input data to a lower-dimensional representation (latent space), and a ''decoder'' network that reconstructs the input from this representation.

The training process involves presenting the model with input data and requiring it to reconstruct the same data as closely as possible. The [[loss function]] used during training typically penalizes the difference between the original input and the reconstructed output (e.g. [[mean squared error]]). By minimizing this reconstruction error, the autoencoder learns a meaningful representation of the data in its [[latent space]].

=== Contrastive self-supervised learning ===
For a [[binary classification]] task, [[Training, validation, and test data sets|training data]] can be divided into positive examples and negative examples. Positive examples are those that match the target. For example, if training a classifier to identify birds, the positive training data would include images that contain birds. Negative examples would be images that do not.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Demystifying a key self-supervised learning technique: Non-contrastive learning|url=https://ai.facebook.com/blog/demystifying-a-key-self-supervised-learning-technique-non-contrastive-learning/|access-date=5 October 2021|website=ai.facebook.com}}</ref> Contrastive self-supervised learning uses both positive and negative examples. The loss function in contrastive learning is used to minimize the distance between positive sample pairs, while maximizing the distance between negative sample pairs.<ref name=":0" />

An early example uses a pair of 1-dimensional [[convolutional neural network]]s to process a pair of images and maximize their agreement.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Becker |first1=Suzanna |last2=Hinton |first2=Geoffrey E. |date=January 1992 |title=Self-organizing neural network that discovers surfaces in random-dot stereograms |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/355161a0 |journal=Nature |volume=355 |issue=6356 |pages=161–163 |doi=10.1038/355161a0 |pmid=1729650 |bibcode=1992Natur.355..161B |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

[[Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training]] (CLIP) allows joint pretraining of a text encoder and an image encoder, such that a matching image-text pair have image encoding vector and text encoding vector that span a small angle (having a large [[cosine similarity]]).

InfoNCE (Noise-Contrastive Estimation)<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Oord |first1=Aaron van den |title=Representation Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding |date=22 January 2019 |eprint=1807.03748 |last2=Li |first2=Yazhe |last3=Vinyals |first3=Oriol |class=cs.LG }}</ref> is a method to optimize two models jointly, based on Noise Contrastive Estimation (NCE).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gutmann |first1=Michael |last2=Hyvärinen |first2=Aapo |date=31 March 2010 |title=Noise-contrastive estimation: A new estimation principle for unnormalized statistical models |url=https://proceedings.mlr.press/v9/gutmann10a |journal=Proceedings of the Thirteenth International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics |publisher=JMLR Workshop and Conference Proceedings |pages=297–304}}</ref> Given a set <math>X=\left\{x_1, \ldots x_N\right\}</math> of <math>N</math> random samples containing one positive sample from <math>p\left(x_{t+k} \mid c_t\right)</math> and <math>N-1</math> negative samples from the 'proposal' distribution <math>p\left(x_{t+k}\right)</math>, it minimizes the following loss function:

<math display="block">
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{N}}=-\mathbb{E}_{X} \left[\log \frac{f_k\left(x_{t+k}, c_t\right)}{\sum_{x_j \in X} f_k\left(x_j, c_t\right)}\right]
</math>

=== Non-contrastive self-supervised learning ===
Non-contrastive self-supervised learning (NCSSL) uses only positive examples. Counterintuitively, NCSSL converges on a useful local minimum rather than reaching a trivial solution, with zero loss. For the example of binary classification, it would trivially learn to classify each example as positive. Effective NCSSL requires an extra predictor on the online side that does not [[Backpropagation|back-propagate]] on the target side.<ref name=":0" />

=== Joint-Embedding and Predictive Architectures ===
A major class of self-supervised learning moves beyond contrastive pairs, instead maximizing the agreement between views while preventing collapse through statistical constraints. Rooted in Deep Canonical Correlation Analysis (Deep CCA),<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Andrew |first1=Galen |last2=Arora |first2=Raman |last3=Bilmes |first3=Jeff |last4=Livescu |first4=Karen |date=26 May 2013 |title=Deep Canonical Correlation Analysis |url=https://proceedings.mlr.press/v28/andrew13.html |journal=Proceedings of the 30th International Conference on Machine Learning |publisher=PMLR |pages=1247–1255}}</ref> this approach includes Joint-Embedding Architectures (JEA) like Barlow Twins<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zbontar |first1=Jure |last2=Jing |first2=Li |last3=Misra |first3=Ishan |last4=LeCun |first4=Yann |last5=Deny |first5=Stephane |date=1 July 2021 |title=Barlow Twins: Self-Supervised Learning via Redundancy Reduction |url=https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/zbontar21a.html |journal=Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning |publisher=PMLR |pages=12310–12320}}</ref> and VICReg,<ref>{{Cite arXiv |last1=Bardes |first1=Adrien |last2=Ponce |first2=Jean |last3=LeCun |first3=Yann |date=11 May 2021 |title=VICReg: Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization for Self-Supervised Learning |class=cs.CV |eprint=2105.04906v3 }}</ref> which enforce covariance constraints to learn invariant representations without negative sampling. Deep Latent Variable Path Modelling (DLVPM)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ing |first1=Alex |last2=Andrades |first2=Alvaro |last3=Cosenza |first3=Marco Raffaele |last4=Korbel |first4=Jan O. |date=July 2025 |title=Integrating multimodal cancer data using deep latent variable path modelling |journal=Nature Machine Intelligence |volume=7 |issue=7 |pages=1053–1075 |doi=10.1038/s42256-025-01052-4 |pmid=40709098 |pmc=12283373 |issn=2522-5839}}</ref> generalizes this to multimodal systems, using path models to enforce correlation and orthogonality across diverse data types.

In 2022 [[Yann LeCun]] introduced Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) as a step towards decision making, reasoning, and autonomous human intelligence in machines, including self-improvement through autonomous learning. Founded in representation learning, LeCun included the concept of a “[[World model (artificial intelligence)|world model]]” in JEPA which aims to enable machines to replicate human intellect by providing machines with a concept for the world in which they exist.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=LeCun|first=Yann|date=27 June 2022|title=A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence|url=https://openreview.net/pdf?id=BZ5a1r-kVsf|journal=OpenReview}}</ref> 

Unlike autoencoders, JEPAs operate entirely in latent space, avoiding pixel-level noise to focus on semantic structure. Rather than just learning invariance, JEPAs learn by predicting masked latent representations from visible context.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Assran |first1=Mahmoud |title=Self-Supervised Learning from Images with a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture |date=13 April 2023 |eprint=2301.08243 |last2=Duval |first2=Quentin |last3=Misra |first3=Ishan |last4=Bojanowski |first4=Piotr |last5=Vincent |first5=Pascal |last6=Rabbat |first6=Michael |last7=LeCun |first7=Yann |last8=Ballas |first8=Nicolas |class=cs.CV }}</ref> JEPA has been applied to domains such as image analysis,<ref>{{cite arXiv|title=Learning and Leveraging World Models in Visual Representation Learning|eprint=2403.00504|first1=Quentin|last1=Garrido|first2=Mahmoud|last2=Assran|first3=Nicolas|last3=Ballas|first4=Adrien|last4=Bardes|first5=Laurent|last5=Najman|first6=Yann|last6=LeCun |date=2024 |class=cs.CV }}</ref> audio processing,<ref>{{cite arXiv|title=A-JEPA: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture Can Listen|eprint=2311.15830|first1=Zhengcong|last1=Fei|first2=Mingyuan|last2=Fan|first3=Junshi|last3=Huang |date=2023 |class=cs.SD }}</ref> and motion in images and video.<ref>{{cite arXiv|title=MC-JEPA: A Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Self-Supervised Learning of Motion and Content Features|eprint=2307.12698|first1=Adrien|last1=Bardes|first2=Jean|last2=Ponce|first3=Yann|last3=LeCun |date=2023 |class=cs.CV }}</ref>

== Comparison with other forms of machine learning ==
SSL belongs to supervised learning methods insofar as the goal is to generate a classified output from the input. At the same time, however, it does not require the explicit use of labeled input-output pairs. Instead, correlations, metadata embedded in the data, or [[domain knowledge]] present in the input are implicitly and autonomously extracted from the data. These supervisory signals, extracted from the data, can then be used for training.<ref name="auto3"/>

SSL is similar to unsupervised learning in that it does not require labels in the sample data. Unlike unsupervised learning, however, learning is not done using inherent data structures.

[[Semi-supervised learning]] combines supervised and unsupervised learning, requiring only a small portion of the learning data be [[Labeled data|labeled]].<ref name="auto1"/>

In [[transfer learning]], a model designed for one task is reused on a different task.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Littwin|first1=Etai|last2=Wolf|first2=Lior|title=2016 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) |chapter=The Multiverse Loss for Robust Transfer Learning |date=June 2016|chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2016.429|pages=3957–3966|publisher=IEEE|doi=10.1109/cvpr.2016.429|arxiv=1511.09033|isbn=978-1-4673-8851-1|s2cid=6517610}}</ref>

Training an [[autoencoder]] intrinsically constitutes a self-supervised process, because the output pattern needs to become an optimal reconstruction of the input pattern itself. However, in current jargon, the term 'self-supervised' often refers to tasks based on a pretext-task training setup. This involves the (human) design of such pretext task(s), unlike 
the case of fully self-contained autoencoder training.<ref name=":17"/>

In [[reinforcement learning]], self-supervising learning from a combination of losses can create abstract representations where only the most important information about the state are kept in a compressed way.<ref>{{Cite conference|last1=Francois-Lavet|first1=Vincent|last2=Bengio|first2=Yoshua|last3=Precup|first3=Doina|last4=Pineau|first4=Joelle|date=2019|title=Combined Reinforcement Learning via Abstract Representations| book-title=Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence|arxiv=1809.04506}}</ref>

== Examples ==
Self-supervised learning is particularly suitable for speech recognition. For example, [[Facebook]] developed ''wav2vec'', a self-supervised algorithm, to perform speech recognition using two deep [[convolutional neural networks]] that build on each other.<ref name="auto"/>

[[Google]]'s [[BERT (language model)|Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers]] (BERT) model is used to better understand the context of search queries.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Open Sourcing BERT: State-of-the-Art Pre-training for Natural Language Processing|url=https://ai.googleblog.com/2018/11/open-sourcing-bert-state-of-art-pre.html|access-date=9 June 2021|website=Google AI Blog|date=2 November 2018 }}</ref>

[[OpenAI]]'s [[GPT-3]] is an autoregressive [[language model]] that can be used in language processing. It can be used to translate texts or answer questions, among other things.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Wilcox|first1=Ethan|last2=Qian|first2=Peng|last3=Futrell|first3=Richard|last4=Kohita|first4=Ryosuke|last5=Levy|first5=Roger|last6=Ballesteros|first6=Miguel|chapter=Structural Supervision Improves Few-Shot Learning and Syntactic Generalization in Neural Language Models |date=2020|title=Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)|chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.18653/v1/2020.emnlp-main.375|pages=4640–4652|location=Stroudsburg, PA, USA|publisher=Association for Computational Linguistics|doi=10.18653/v1/2020.emnlp-main.375|arxiv=2010.05725|s2cid=222291675}}</ref>

''Bootstrap Your Own Latent'' (BYOL) is a NCSSL that produced excellent results on [[ImageNet]] and on transfer and semi-supervised benchmarks.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Grill|first1=Jean-Bastien|last2=Strub|first2=Florian|last3=Altché|first3=Florent|last4=Tallec|first4=Corentin|last5=Richemond|first5=Pierre H.|last6=Buchatskaya|first6=Elena|last7=Doersch|first7=Carl|last8=Pires|first8=Bernardo Avila|last9=Guo|first9=Zhaohan Daniel|last10=Azar|first10=Mohammad Gheshlaghi|last11=Piot|first11=Bilal|date=10 September 2020|title=Bootstrap your own latent: A new approach to self-supervised Learning|class=cs.LG|eprint=2006.07733}}</ref>

The [[Yarowsky algorithm]] is an example of self-supervised learning in [[natural language processing]]. From a small number of labeled examples, it learns to predict which [[word sense disambiguation|word sense]] of a [[polysemy|polysemous]] word is being used at a given point in text.

DirectPred is a NCSSL that directly sets the predictor weights instead of learning it via typical [[gradient descent]].<ref name=":0" />

Self-GenomeNet is an example of self-supervised learning in genomics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gündüz |first1=Hüseyin Anil |last2=Binder |first2=Martin |last3=To |first3=Xiao-Yin |last4=Mreches |first4=René |last5=Bischl |first5=Bernd |last6=McHardy |first6=Alice C. |last7=Münch |first7=Philipp C. |last8=Rezaei |first8=Mina |date=11 September 2023 |title=A self-supervised deep learning method for data-efficient training in genomics |journal=Communications Biology |volume=6 |issue=1 |page=928 |doi=10.1038/s42003-023-05310-2 |issn=2399-3642|doi-access=free |pmid=37696966 |pmc=10495322 }}</ref>

SelfAPR is an example of self-supervised learning applied to [[automatic bug fixing|automated program repair]], where a neural model is trained on perturbations of a previous version of the program under repair and uses test execution diagnostics to synthesize patches.<ref>{{cite book |last1= Ye |first1= He |last2= Martinez |first2= Matias |last3= Luo |first3= Xiapu |last4= Zhang |first4= Tao |last5= Monperrus |first5= Martin |chapter= SelfAPR: Self-supervised Program Repair with Test Execution Diagnostics |title= Proceedings of the 37th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering |date= 2022 |pages= 1–13 |chapter-url= https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3551349.3556926 |access-date= 28 May 2026 |doi= 10.1145/3551349.3556926 |isbn= 978-1-4503-9475-8 }}</ref>

Self-supervised learning continues to gain prominence as a new approach across diverse fields. Its ability to leverage unlabeled data effectively opens new possibilities for advancement in machine learning, especially in data-driven application domains.
